newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil civil service pay hike.
newsitem.headline: Brazil civil service pay hike.

text.p: Brazil's highest court Tribunal late Wednesday granted a 28.9 percent wage hike to 11 civil servants, who had argued that they deserved the same pay rise awarded to the armed services in 1993.

The ruling by the Supreme Federal Tribunal is expected to encourage up to a million other past and present public workers to demand the same salary adjustment, which would cost the federal government billions of dollars a year in extra payroll costs at a time when it is trying to slash expenditures.

Based on interviews with political analysts and legal experts, Reuters has compiled the following list of likely strategies that could be adopted by the civil service and the government in reaction to the high court ruling.

* The 11 civil servants who won in court on Wednesday received a pay rise on salaries retroactive to the date they launched their case in July 1993. They are now expected to launch and win a separate case against the government to sue for the full 28.9 percent salary adjustment retroactive to February 1993, when the pay hike was granted to the military.

* Their victory will encourage up to one million past and present civil servants to unite by sector and launch separate cases for existing and retroactive wage hikes. They are widely expected to win both cases.
* A 28.9 percent pay hike on all existing federal salaries is estimated to cost the government an extra $5.0 billion a year, while a once-off backpay adjustment would cost about $20 billion.

* Although workers are expected to win, the legal battle could take at least three years - given the case load and Brazil's slow judicial process - and the goverment might not have to pay the full amount for an additional three years.
BRASILIA - DELAY TACTICS AND GET TOUGH POLICIES
Senior Federal government officials have privately conceded they will eventually have to grant wage hikes to all federal workers. But Brasilia has some cards up its sleeve.
* First, the government can now use the court ruling as an excuse to use more of its discretionay powers and be more aggressive in curbing payroll costs.
* The government may delay or cancel a 10 percent salary hike for civil servants that was tentatively planned to be introduced later this year. Future wage hikes could also be withheld.

* Some 20,000 federal workers whose jobs are not fully protected by the constitution could be fired to slash costs. An additional 30,000 employees known as "double dippers" because they receive full pay benefits in two job categories might be forced to give up one full salary.

* The government will do all it can to see that the wheels of Brazilian justice turn as slowly as they normally do to delay the inevitable fiscal impact of the wage hikes. Brazilian labor disputes are rarely resolved before a period of two years and often delay as long as six years or more.
* The government's delaying tactics will be helped by the fact that the high court's ruling was not unanimous but passed by a tight 6-4 vote.
* The high court's ruling was not expected to have a significant fiscal impact in 1997.
* Pro-government allies in Congress will use the ruling to call attention to the need for urgent passage of pension and civil service reforms.
